reference.title: Appearance: What does he / she look like?
rows: She has curly red hair. She has long straight hair. She has short blonde hair.
He has a beard and a moustache.
He’s very tall and thin. He’s medium height and very slim. He’s quite short and a bit overweight.

reference.title: Using two adjectives together
reference.text: Adjectives go in this order: size → style → colour + noun. She has long straight blonde hair. He has big brown eyes.

reference.title: thin or slim? fat or overweight?
reference.text: Thin and slim are both the opposite of fat, but slim = thin in an attractive way. Fat is not very polite. It is more polite to say someone is (a bit) overweight.

reference.title: handsome or beautiful?
reference.text: Handsome is used for men, beautiful for women; good-looking and attractive are used for both men and women.

reference.title: Personality: What’s he / she like?
rows: is friendly and good to other people
is quick at learning and understanding things
can’t talk easily to people he / she doesn’t know

reference.title: What does she look like? What is she like?
reference.text: What does she look like? = Tell me about her appearance (Is she tall / short? What colour hair does she have?). What is she like? = Tell me what kind of person she is (Is she friendly? Is she shy?).

reference.wrong: What is your sister look like?
reference.right: What does your sister look like?
reference.why: look like is a verb: the question needs does.

tasks.instruction: Ask and answer questions about a member of your family or a good friend
tasks.note: VB ACTIVATION → разговор с ИИ

exercises.situation: You are a classmate in an English class (level: pre-intermediate). You and the student talk about members of your families or good friends. Your person: your sister Marta, 29 – quite tall and slim, with short dark curly hair and brown eyes; she is talkative, generous and very funny, but a bit lazy at home. First answer the student’s questions about Marta: What does she look like? (appearance) and What’s she like? (personality). Give short, natural answers with the vocabulary of the lesson (tall, short, medium height, slim, thin, a bit overweight, long / short, straight / curly, dark / blonde / red hair, beard, moustache, bald; friendly, talkative, quiet, generous, mean, kind, lazy, hard-working, funny, serious, clever, shy, extrovert). If the student mixes up the questions (e.g. asks What is she like? but means appearance), answer the question they actually asked, so they notice. Then ask about their person: Who are you going to tell me about? What does he / she look like? What’s he / she like? Ask one follow-up question. If the student says fat, say gently that a bit overweight is more polite.

describes personality with at least 3 adjectives from the lesson
uses two adjectives in the right order (size → style → colour: long straight hair)

reference.title: Present simple
rows: My brother works in the city centre.
My parents don’t live near here.
Yes, I do. / No, I don’t.
Yes, he does. / No, he doesn’t.

reference.text: We use the present simple for things we do every day / week / year, or which are generally true or always happen. Use don’t / doesn’t in negatives and do / does in questions: after them the verb has no -s.

reference.title: Spelling: he / she / it
rows: add -es after ch, s, sh, x

reference.title: Adverbs and expressions of frequency
rows: We often go out on Friday night.
She doesn’t usually study at weekends.
She gets up early every day.
We have English classes twice a week.

reference.title: Word order
reference.text: always, usually, often, sometimes, hardly ever, never go before the main verb, but after be: She’s never ill. Expressions like every day, once a week, twice a month usually go at the end of the sentence.

reference.why: Adverbs of frequency go after be.
never is already negative: use a positive verb with it.
Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb.
After does the verb has no -s.

reference.title: Describing yourself
reference.text: A profile has five paragraphs: 1 name, age, nationality (My name’s… Everyone calls me…) 2 work / study, family (I’m going to tell you about myself. I live with…) 3 physical appearance (As you can see from the photo… My father always says…) 4 personality (I think I’m a… person. My friends say…) 5 hobbies and interests (When I’m not in class… When I can, I like…). Age: I’m 21 (years old), not I have 21 years.

tasks.note: SB 1d; «find the information» → Blank по пунктам (5 пунктов книги, partner — на двух строках). Ответы по тексту статьи (MODEL)
tasks.context: Please date my dad! ‘So, how was the date?’ You probably think this is a parent asking the question to their child. But many children are now helping their single parents find love, too. Clint Bouchez, a 52-year-old businessman from Reigate, Surrey, got divorced ten years ago. His daughter, 26-year-old Charlotte, doesn’t want her dad to end up alone – her mum remarried five years ago, and Charlotte has a boyfriend. Charlotte and Clint are very close. They often go out together in the evening, they’re planning a trip to India for later in the year, and they’re both Bruce Springsteen fans. But Charlotte thinks that Clint needs a new partner, and he agrees. ‘My dad is the perfect man,’ she says. ‘He’s warm, he’s generous, he knows how to look after a woman, how to treat a woman. He’s a gentleman. He’s always the one who pays on dates. He’s romantic and he’s fun. I don’t mind spending Friday and Saturday nights with my dad and that says a lot – I’m only 26.’ Dating in the 21st century is very different from when Clint was young. Internet dating has changed everything. ‘It’s difficult now just to walk over to a woman and ask her “Can I buy you a drink?”’ he says. ‘Before, when you met people face to face, there was sometimes a “spark”, a feeling of romantic destiny – you don’t get that from someone’s profile picture.’ Charlotte wrote Clint’s dating profile for an online dating website. Clint would like to meet a woman who works, preferably a businesswoman. Someone who’s independent, but funny and clever. He has had several dates, but none of the women were right for him. He and Charlotte are still looking. ‘I’m always hopeful,’ he says. ‘I really believe that sooner or later I’m going to find “the one”.’

tasks.context: Please date my dad! ‘So, how was the date?’ You probably think this is a parent asking the question to their child. But many children are now helping their single parents find love, too. Clint Bouchez, a 52-year-old businessman from Reigate, Surrey, got divorced ten years ago. His daughter, 26-year-old Charlotte, doesn’t want her dad to end up alone – her mum remarried five years ago, and Charlotte has a boyfriend. Charlotte and Clint are very close. They often go out together in the evening, they’re planning a trip to India for later in the year, and they’re both Bruce Springsteen fans. But Charlotte thinks that Clint needs a new partner, and he agrees. ‘My dad is the perfect man,’ she says. ‘He’s warm, he’s generous, he knows how to look after a woman, how to treat a woman. He’s a gentleman. He’s always the one who pays on dates. He’s romantic and he’s fun. I don’t mind spending Friday and Saturday nights with my dad and that says a lot – I’m only 26.’ Dating in the 21st century is very different from when Clint was young. Internet dating has changed everything. ‘It’s difficult now just to walk over to a woman and ask her “Can I buy you a drink?”’ he says. ‘Before, when you met people face to face, there was sometimes a “spark”, a feeling of romantic destiny – you don’t get that from someone’s profile picture.’ Charlotte wrote Clint’s dating profile for an online dating website. Clint would like to meet a woman who works, preferably a businesswoman. Someone who’s independent, but funny and clever. He has had several dates, but none of the women were right for him. He and Charlotte are still looking. ‘I’m always hopeful,’ he says. ‘I really believe that sooner or later I’m going to find “the one”.’

exercises.prompt: Answer the questions about the article in 1–2 sentences each.
questions: Why does Charlotte want to find Clint a partner?
How do we know that Charlotte and Clint are close?
What was dating like when Clint was young?
How does Clint find dates now, and how has Charlotte helped him?
criteria: 1: she doesn’t want him to end up alone – her mum has remarried and she has a boyfriend
2: they often go out together in the evening, they’re planning a trip to India, and they both like Bruce Springsteen
3: people met face to face, you could walk over to a woman and offer her a drink, and there was sometimes a ‘spark’
4: he uses internet / online dating; Charlotte wrote his dating profile
answers are the student’s own sentences, not whole lines copied from the article

tasks.instruction: Communication: A date for Clint. Ask and answer questions about two possible dates for Clint
tasks.note: SB 3c + Communication 1B (A p.102, B p.108) + 3d «class vote»: ученик — A (Maggie), ИИ — B (Tessa). Фото → описание

exercises.situation: Communication activity ‘A date for Clint’ with an English student (pre-intermediate). The student is Student A and has a profile of Maggie; you are Student B and have a profile of Tessa: Tessa Mills, 42, single, a nurse (‘I’m a nurse’). Looks: long blonde hair, smiling (invent a little more if asked: blue eyes, medium height, slim). Personality: fun, talkative, generous. Likes: travelling, going to pop concerts, going out. Doesn’t like: mean men who never pay for dates. The student asks you about Tessa with these questions: What does she look like? How old is she? What’s her status? What does she do? What’s she like? What does she like doing? What kind of men doesn’t she like? Answer with full, natural sentences in the present simple (She’s a nurse. She likes going to pop concerts.). Then ask the student about Maggie, one question at a time: What does she look like? How old is she? What’s her status? What does she do? What’s she like? What does she like doing? What doesn’t she like doing? At the end ask: Who do you think is a better date for Clint, Maggie or Tessa? Why? Give your own opinion too. If the student makes a mistake with -s (she like, does she likes), repeat the sentence correctly in your answer.

exercises.situation: You are a classmate in an English class (level: pre-intermediate). The student describes a single person they know (from a form: name, relationship status, age, job, appearance, personality, likes, doesn’t like), e.g. ‘His name’s Mario, and he’s single. He’s about 30 years old.’ Listen and ask for more information about anything missing (What does he look like? What’s he like? What does he like doing? What doesn’t he like?). Give the details only when asked, and let the student ask you questions. At the end ask whether they know anyone for Daniel.
